title: Module 03 opener — Hormones and Peptides for Skin
note: Module opener in the cinematic lane (docs/motion-contract.md § 10b), same look and rules as the Module 1 opener. Script assembled only from approved text (sources below); presenter lines pass the course script review; draft media until the media preview.

script.text: Facial shape depends on fat as much as on collagen. In three lessons you will separate what is known about the skin's own fat, sugar damage to the dermis, weight-loss drugs and the gut from what is still mechanism, marketing or an open question. Most people picture skin fat as one layer under the dermis. There is a second, thinner layer inside the reticular dermis itself, called dermal white adipose tissue. In mice, this layer expands rapidly after a Staphylococcus aureus infection, and its new fat cells release cathelicidin, an antimicrobial peptide. Older mice lose much of that capacity, through TGF-beta signalling. Human skin arranges this fat differently, in small cones around hair follicles, and human acne lesions contain preadipocytes around the follicle that make cathelicidin. What the layer contributes to human skin ageing has not yet been measured. So hold two things apart when you hear about skin fat. The defence story is strong in mice and emerging in people. The ageing story in people is still a proposal.

assets.prompt: Accurate scientific medical illustration: a vertical cross-section block of human skin seen slightly from the side like a textbook plate, centred with generous empty margins. From top to bottom: the epidermis, the papillary and reticular dermis with wavy collagen bundles, and a thick subcutaneous fat layer of rounded yellow fat lobules. Two hair follicles run down through the dermis, and around the lower part of each follicle sits a small cone of fat cells. Inside the lowest part of the reticular dermis runs a distinct thin band of fat cells, separate from the subcutaneous fat below it.

Accurate scientific medical illustration: a close-up round vignette of the lower dermis during a skin infection, centred with generous empty margins. On one side, grape-like clusters of small round bacteria (Staphylococcus aureus). Beside them, a group of newly formed small fat cells, each with a single pale lipid droplet, releases a haze of tiny violet antimicrobial peptide molecules toward the bacteria. Collagen fibres in the background.
